title: What I've Learned from Direct Instruction
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane revisits Direct Instruction (DI) a year after first reviewing Kurt Engelmann's Direct Instruction: A Practitioner's Guide, reaffirming that he has no desire to become a full DI teacher - the approach's lack of participation variety and its requirement to function as a whole-school placement system don't fit his values or context - while explaining in detail three specific DI-derived practices he has genuinely incorporated into his own maths teaching. First is choral response: a simple, low-prep routine (silent think time, a synchronized 'ready, go' signal, unison response) that he now uses in most lessons for 2-4 minutes total, valuing it for engagement, as a rough whole-class check for understanding, and for the variety it adds against other work modes. Second is spreading practice into short chunks across many lessons and weeks rather than concentrating it immediately after initial teaching - Kane notes that a typical DI lesson spends 80-90% of its time on practice and review of prior material, a ratio he treats as an aspirational (if not fully achieved) benchmark, because it builds in retention time and avoids boring students who grasp a skill quickly. Third is deliberately pre-teaching prerequisite skills in short chunks over the months before a new unit begins (e.g., practicing percents ahead of a percent-increase-and-decrease unit), which he reports makes subsequent units go noticeably more smoothly. Kane closes by generalising past his own selective adoption: most teachers know little about DI and would benefit from engaging with its ideas even if, like him, they ultimately decide not to adopt the whole system.
points: Kane's clear boundary: despite learning a great deal from Direct Instruction, he has 'no desire to become a Direct Instruction teacher' - citing its lack of participation variety and its nature as a whole-school placement system, not just a lesson-planning approach.

Practice #1 he has adopted - choral response: a simple silent-think, synchronized 'ready, go' signal, unison-answer routine, now used in most lessons for just 2-4 minutes total, valued for engagement and as a rough whole-class check for understanding.

Practice #2 - short, spaced chunks of practice: rather than concentrating practice immediately after teaching a skill, Kane spreads it across many lessons and weeks; he notes a typical DI lesson spends 80-90% of its time on practice/review of prior material, a ratio he treats as an aspirational benchmark.

Practice #3 - deliberately pre-teaching prerequisite skills in short chunks over the months before a new unit (e.g., practicing percents before a percent-increase/decrease unit), which he reports makes the eventual unit go noticeably more smoothly.

Kane's closing generalisation: 'far too many teachers don't know anything about Direct Instruction, and they would have a lot to learn if they were open to it' - even those who, like him, ultimately reject adopting DI as a whole system.
quotes: I've learned a lot from Direct Instruction but I still have no desire to become a Direct Instruction teacher. DI doesn't provide much variety in how students participate -- it's mostly choral response, cold calling, and written work.
I say, "think in your head, what is 50% of 12?" I pause and let students think. Then I raise my hand above my head, say, "Ready, go", as I say go I bring my hand down, and students say the answer.
Now I use choral response in most lessons. It's quick -- often 2-4 minutes of total time in a lesson.
To put a number on it, a typical Direct Instruction lesson spends about 80-90% of the time practicing and reviewing ideas that have been introduced previously.
The more I do this, the more little skills I find to teach before we start a unit, and the smoother that unit goes.
My opinion is that far too many teachers don't know anything about Direct Instruction, and they would have a lot to learn if they were open to it.
